vignette:
James

James sits in the leather chair across from me with his back straight, hands folded in his lap. At seventy-eight, he maintains the careful posture of someone who has spent decades at a desk, though his frame has grown thinner in recent years. He's been retired from his database administration work for three years now, though he still volunteers part-time at the local library managing their digital archives. It's the only thing, he tells me, that makes the days feel purposeful.

Four years ago, James was diagnosed with acute leukemia. He remembers the morning of the diagnosis with crystalline clarity-the oncologist's face, the way the light fell through the hospital window, the exact words: "You have maybe six months without treatment, possibly longer with it." He was sixty-four then, still working full-time, still married to his sense of control. The treatment was brutal. Six months of chemotherapy that left him vomiting, hairless, terrified. He remembers the night he thought he was dying-fever spiking to 104, his ex-wife Sarah driving him to the emergency room at two in the morning, the feeling that his body had become a foreign country he no longer recognized.

He survived. The cancer went into remission. But something didn't come back with him.

Now, James describes his current life in a voice that sounds almost clinical, as though he's documenting data rather than living it. He wakes at three in the morning most nights, his heart racing, drenched in sweat. In those dark hours, he's convinced the cancer has returned. He lies there cataloging his body for signs-a pain in his chest, a swollen lymph node, a persistent ache. By the time morning comes, he's often cycled through an entire catastrophic narrative: the cancer is back, the doctors missed it, he's dying.

During the day, he avoids his body. He doesn't exercise, though his doctor recommends it. He doesn't attend his grandson's soccer games anymore because sitting in the bleachers with other people feels impossible-he's hypervigilant to every cough around him, every mention of illness. Last month, his daughter mentioned she had a headache, and James found himself unable to be in the same room for the rest of the evening, his mind spiraling into scenarios about what it could mean, what could happen to her.

He's become a creature of routine and isolation. The library work is safe because it's solitary-just him and the databases, systems he can understand and control. He eats the same meals, takes the same walks around his quiet neighborhood at the same time each day, always alert to his physical sensations. Any deviation from routine sends him into a state of anxious vigilance that can last for hours.

What James struggles most to articulate is the fundamental shift in how he experiences time. Before the diagnosis, he lived in a future-oriented way-planning database projects, thinking about retirement, imagining growing old with Sarah. Now, he lives in a perpetual present tense, hyperaware of his breathing, his heartbeat, the sensations in his body that might signal danger. The future feels both impossibly long and impossibly fragile. He'll be seventy-eight, he thinks sometimes, but he might not be seventy-nine.

He tells me he knows, logically, that he's in remission. He's had good scans. But knowing and believing have become two separate things. The body keeps its own counsel, and James's body is convinced that death is always standing just outside his peripheral vision, waiting for the moment he lets his guard down.
